segs.text: Section thirty four. Absorption and distribution interactions. An absorption interaction changes how fast and how much of the object drug reaches the systemic circulation, so bioavailability goes up or down. The gut is the most common site. Two interactions keep the drug in the gut. Complexation or chelation is the tighter bond: levofloxacin, a quinolone, complexes with divalent cations such as calcium, magnesium, aluminum and iron. Adsorption, spelled with a D, is a looser bond: digoxin sticks to cholestyramine, kaolin or acarbose, so less is absorbed. Adsorption with a D is the interaction; absorption with a B is the process it changes. Separating the doses by several hours lets one get through first.

Motility works both ways. Laxatives and cathartics speed transit, so slowly absorbed drugs and controlled release products lose bioavailability. Anticholinergics such as propantheline slow gastric emptying, delaying acetaminophen absorption. H two blockers, antacids and proton pump inhibitors raise gastric p H, and ketoconazole dissolves less at basic p H, so therapy can fail. Antibiotics change gut flora: erythromycin reduces the bacteria that inactivate digoxin, so digoxin rises; for estrogen and progestin birth control, antibiotics reduce the flora needed for enterohepatic circulation, so hormone levels fall and ovulation suppression can fail.

Two more gut interactions are worth knowing. In competition for carrier mediated absorption, the precipitant competes for the same carrier as the object drug; her carrier example is P glycoprotein. Alteration in intestinal blood flow is rare, and motility changes are of more concern. Absorption interactions also happen outside the gut: epinephrine is given with the local anesthetic Novocaine to keep the anesthetic localized.

A distribution interaction happens after absorption. The precipitant pushes the object drug off its binding sites, so more is free, and only free drug reaches targets. Binding stays constant at steady state unless another compound competes for the sites. Valproic acid, added for breakthrough seizures, binds plasma proteins better than phenytoin and displaces it; phenytoin has a narrow therapeutic index, so more free phenytoin can cause side effects. Aspirin in turn displaces valproic acid, making it the object drug.

Tissue binding works the same way. Digoxin has a very high volume of distribution and binds muscle, not bone. Quinidine, given for breakthrough arrhythmias, has an even higher volume of distribution, displaces digoxin from muscle and binds there. Free digoxin rises, and with its narrow therapeutic index toxicity can be enhanced. Displacement changes free drug, not metabolism, so it is not enzyme induction.
